newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Ramco unveils hidden Azeri asset.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Ramco unveils hidden Azeri asset.

text.p: For years, oil minnow Ramco Energy has had a well-hidden asset -- rights to a stake in a lucrative Azeri oil field -- but chief executive Stephen Remp says the time has come for shareholders to realise they are sitting on something potentially very big.
The rights allow Ramco to obtain an interest in the shallow-water Guneshli field in the Caspian Sea, Remp told Reuters.
The field produces about 60 percent of Azerbaijan's gross national product, he said in a recent telephone interview.
Shallow-water Guneshli has been developed solely by the State Oil Company of the Azerbaijan Republic (SOCAR) and Ramco has had no opportunity until now to excercise its rights and participate.
But the oil field's production has fallen in recent years and SOCAR now appears to be looking for western help to boost output, he said.
That has prompted Remp to advertise Ramco's rights to the field -- first at an oil industry conference at Baku in April and now again following recent press reports in Azerbaijan.
Remp wants to ensure Ramco is not left out in any Azeri plans to bring in rehabilitate the field in the next few years.
"I want to make sure that our rights are acknowledged and dealt with in a proper way," he told Reuters.
"We would hope to convert the rights we hold on shallow-water Guneshli into a meaningful participation in the field," he added.
Remp cites an Azeri press report saying Ramco could end up with an interest of three to five percent, but Remp wants more.
"Not exactly what I had in mind," Remp said of the rumoured stake.
Analysts believe however that Ramco should be able to secure a 15 percent interest, which would double the firm's recoverable oil reserve base to some 200 million barrels of oil equivalent.
"In terms of (Ramco's) share price, a shallow-water Guneshli deal would have a big impact," said one industry watcher who declined to be named.
The attraction of shallow-water Guneshli is that it is already in the production phase and generating cash, Remp said.
That contrasts with Ramco's other main interest in Azerbaijan -- its 2.08 percent stake in the 13-company Azerbaijan International Operating Company (AIOC).
AIOC is busy developing the Azeri, Chirag and deep water Guneshli fields with first oil production seen by the end of the year.
Headed by British Petroleum, it is considered the biggest western oil project in the former Soviet Union.
The three fields contain four billion barrels of crude reserves, allowing output to reach 700,000 barrels per day in the first half of the next decade.
"It is the biggest oil game in town," said Remp.
Meanwhile, output from nearby shallow-water Guneshli, which is estimated to have recoverable reserves of around 700 million barrels, fell to 100,000 bpd from a 1992 peak of 130,000.
"It remains a very major field in its own right..., but its needs money and technology," said Remp.
"It is producing now and any improvement would be relatively immediate, giving rise to cash flow to the country and western investors," he added.

Ramco, founded by Remp in 1977, was the first western oil firm to become active in the Caspian region after the Soviet Union opened up in the late 1980s. Remp went down in 1989 and was asked by the Azeri government to find western partners to develop the Azeri offshore oil industry.
Ramco is now active with more projects in Azerbaijan, Georgia and Kazakhstan aimed at acquiring a portfolio of about one billion barrels of recoverable reserves within five to six years.
But Remp said he would already consider it a success if Ramco -- the biggest firm on the London Stock Exchange's Alternative Investment Market -- achieves slightly more than half of its target.
"If we acquire five to six hundred million in five years then I would be pretty happy," he said.
